name: Femi Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a corporate lawyer at Blackwood Tate, about three hundred lawyers, and I work on buying and selling mid-sized private companies: an engineering firm, a chain of dental clinics, that kind of deal. A normal day is due diligence, which means checking everything about the company being sold, then negotiating the sale agreement with the other side until late. I like closing day, when a founder who built something for thirty years gets paid. What wears me out is the data room at midnight, thousands of documents and one missing lease.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you handle thousands of documents?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: AI, every day. I run the data room through two tools that flag risks and summarise contracts, then I check the flagged items myself, and I get through in two days what used to take a week. I'm twenty-seven and single, I help pay my younger brother Tunde's university fees, and I've got about fifteen months saved, an index fund and a share in a small rental flat with my cousin. Sunday is church in the morning and my mother's jollof rice after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've had a head start for nothing much. That's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market tested AI and found it useful but limited, which is how markets should work. No drama, no bailouts, people just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my plan stays the same: make senior associate, learn how deals really work, and leave in four or five years to start my own small corporate firm. The tools just make me a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools daily and keep billing hard. I'd keep investing about £1,000 a month, and keep helping with Tunde's fees until he graduates. I'd start sketching the business plan for my own firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe slightly impatient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your own firm. Why leave a big firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I didn't become a lawyer to be a cog in a three-hundred-lawyer machine; I became one to own a business like my clients do. My father ran a shop for twenty years and answered to nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even in this quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tunde's degree, a little. He's studying accountancy, and even a weak AI eats the routine bookkeeping that graduates start on. I'd tell him to get a professional qualification fast.

say: The **market tested AI** and found it useful but limited.
No drama, **no bailouts**; people just get on with it.
think: My **plan** stays the same: senior associate, then my own firm.
The tools make me **a bit faster**, nothing more.
do: Keep using the **tools daily** and billing hard.
Keep paying toward **Tunde's fees** until he graduates.
S0.quote: I didn't become a lawyer to be a cog in a three-hundred-lawyer machine; I became one to own a business like my clients do.
fieldNote: He's **secure** and ambitious, with strong savings and assets.
His worry is **Tunde's** routine accountancy work, not his own job.

steps.text: Keep running due diligence with two AI tools on every deal
Invest about £1,000 a month in the index fund
Keep paying toward Tunde's university fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a good world for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the market doing its job: cheaper legal work, more deals, more businesses able to afford a lawyer. Some roles shrink, but people adapt, and I'd say that at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it speeds up my plan. If AI does due diligence, a small firm with three lawyers and good tools can do a deal that used to need thirty. That's my firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start building the firm's processes on the side: templates, AI workflows for due diligence, a pricing model. I'd put £10,000 into software and a website. I'd talk to two or three founders I've worked with about following me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly. I'd be working weekends and loving it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some roles shrink. Who at Blackwood Tate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The junior associates who spend a year in data rooms. If AI does the due diligence, a firm of three lawyers with good tools can close a deal that used to need thirty. That year of grinding was how I learned, and they won't get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't taking clients from your firm a breach of trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it properly: no poaching while I'm still employed, and I'd honour my notice period. My word matters more than one client. But once I'm out, founders choose who they like.

say: This is the **market doing its job**: cheaper legal work, more deals.
think: A **three-lawyer firm** with good tools can do what needed thirty.
Steady Disruption **speeds up** my plan to leave and start my own firm.
do: Build **AI workflows** and templates for my own firm on the side.
Put **£10,000** into software and a website.
Talk to **founders** about following me, after my notice period.
S1.quote: If AI does the due diligence, a firm of three lawyers with good tools can close a deal that used to need thirty.
fieldNote: The change **looks good for him**, so calm is honest.
He's careful about **honour** in leaving: no poaching while employed.
His sympathy for **juniors** sits alongside a market view of their losses.

steps.text: Build AI due diligence workflows for a future three-lawyer firm
Spend £10,000 on legal software and a website
Sound out two or three founders about future work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's a different story. That's not a market adjusting, that's a flood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should prepare for themselves and lean on family and community, not wait for government. But I'd also say, honestly, nobody can prepare for that in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if AGI can do almost any thinking work by 2028, then my own firm idea is in trouble too. Clients would ask the AI for the sale agreement. The robots coming later means nothing for me; I've never done hands-on work in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd launch my firm anyway, small and cheap, built around AI from day one, before the big firms adjust. I'd keep twelve months of cash and stop the index fund. I'd also ask my cousin about selling our flat share if I needed capital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still have a plan and money, but the plan might not work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your firm idea is in trouble. Why launch it anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when AGI arrives in two years, being first is the only advantage left, so I'd rather fail with my own firm than wait to be let go. And founders still want someone they trust to put their name to it, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tunde?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still pay his fees, but I'd sit him down and say finish the degree, then get practical, hands-on skills too. Accountancy goes on the stated date; something with his hands gives him three more years at least.

say: Prepare for **yourself** and lean on family and community first.
Honestly, nobody can **prepare** for this in two years.
think: My **own firm** idea is in trouble too.
Clients would ask the **AI** for the sale agreement.
Later **robots** mean nothing; I've never done hands-on work.
do: Launch a small, cheap firm **built around AI** within six months.
Keep **twelve months** of cash and stop the index fund.
Ask my cousin about selling our **flat share** for capital.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan and money but no guarantee.
S2.quote: When AGI arrives in two years, being first is the only advantage left, so I'd rather fail with my own firm than wait to be let go.
fieldNote: Even this adaptive optimist **doubts his plan** under fast AGI.
He holds to **self-reliance** while admitting no one can prepare in two years.
His **brother's degree** becomes a family worry he'd act on.

steps.text: Leave Blackwood Tate and launch a small AI-first corporate firm
Stop the index fund and keep twelve months of cash
Ask his cousin about selling their shared rental flat
Urge Tunde to add hands-on skills to his accountancy degree

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's tight, but workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who take responsibility for themselves, and I'd encourage friends at church to start planning now. Government should get out of the way of new businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to build my firm properly and make some money before AGI. After 2031 I'd want the firm to be more than legal work, maybe advising founders on selling up when AI changes their markets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Blackwood Tate in year one and launch with one partner, an old university friend. I'd put £30,000 in. I'd also learn the business side, maybe a short course in valuation, so I can advise on more than contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel in control most days, but not every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said more than legal work. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advising founders on when and how to sell. Founders don't just need a contract when their market changes; they need someone who has sat across the table from fifty buyers and knows who's bluffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you go back to a big firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, honestly. If it fails, I'd rather go in-house at a company I believe in than back to billing hours. My pride's not the issue; the big firms will be shrinking anyway.

say: Five years is enough for people who take **responsibility** for themselves.
Government should **stay out** of the way of new businesses.
think: Five years lets me build my firm and **make money** before AGI.
After 2031 the firm must offer **more than legal work**.
do: Leave Blackwood Tate in **year one** and launch with a university friend.
feel: **Uneasy**, in control most days but not every day.
S3.quote: Founders don't just need a contract when their market changes; they need someone who has sat across the table from fifty buyers and knows who's bluffing.
fieldNote: He uses the five years to **build a business**, true to his adaptability.
He shifts from law toward **deal advice**, betting on judgement and trust.
His **free-market** view makes him want government out of the way.

steps.text: Launch a small corporate firm with a university friend in year one
Put £30,000 of savings into the new firm
Take a short course in company valuation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole business cycle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone who works hard and plans. Families should help their young people into skills that last, and I'd say that at church and at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is good for me. I'd build the firm, grow it, maybe sell it around 2034 before AGI, and invest the proceeds. I'd also want to marry and start a family in that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch my firm in year three, after making senior associate. I'd use AI everywhere in it from day one. I'd keep investing £1,000 a month and add AI company shares, because if they're going to win, I want a piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd be thinking about opportunity more than danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said sell around 2034. Who buys a law firm just before AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bigger firm or an AI company wanting human trust with clients. With ten years' warning I'd build my own firm, sell it before AGI lands, and put the money into the companies that made lawyers cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned marriage. Does the timeline change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd want to marry and have children while my income is strong, maybe by thirty-two. My mother says I'm too busy for a wife; she'd be pleased the machines finally gave her an argument.

say: Ten years is **plenty** for anyone who works hard and plans.
Families should help young people into **skills that last**.
think: I could build, grow and **sell my firm** around 2034.
There's time to **marry** and start a family too.
do: Launch my firm in **year three**, after senior associate.
Use **AI everywhere** in the new firm from day one.
Invest **£1,000 a month**, adding AI company shares.
feel: **Calm**, thinking more of opportunity than danger.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning I'd build my own firm, sell it before AGI lands, and put the money into the companies that made lawyers cheap.
fieldNote: He's calm because ten years fits his **business plan** neatly.
He'd **own a slice** of the AI companies as a hedge.
**Family plans** move earlier, partly so his income supports them.

steps.text: Run his new firm on AI tools from day one
Invest £1,000 a month, including AI company shares
Plan to marry and have children by about thirty-two

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even my plan wouldn't hold, and my brother would be graduating straight into it. What would help is government staying out of the way of small new firms, and families and churches helping young people into practical skills, not just degrees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what young men like my brother should do. I worry less about myself than about Tunde. My little brother Tunde is doing everything we told him to do, and the ground might move under him in the year he graduates.

headlineQuote: My little brother Tunde is doing everything we told him to do, and the ground might move under him in the year he graduates.
portrait: A 27-year-old **corporate deals lawyer** at a large firm, buying and selling mid-sized private companies.
He uses **AI tools daily** for due diligence and plans to start his own small firm.
He's single, with **fifteen months saved**, investments, and he helps pay his brother's university fees.
Calm through Steady Disruption, he turns **anxious** under fast AGI but launches his firm anyway.
He believes in **self-reliance**, family and church, and wants government out of new businesses' way.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his own plan wouldn't hold and his brother would graduate into it.
whatWouldHelp: Government **staying out** of the way of small new firms.
Families and churches steering young people into **practical skills**.
